title: Quantifying and Probing Multipartite Entanglement via Minimum Entanglement Drop
authors: Dong-Dong Dong, Xue-Ke Song, Liu Ye, Dong Wang
abstract: Quantifying genuine multipartite entanglement remains a significant challenge. We propose a multipartite entanglement monotone defined by the minimum entanglement drop -- the reduction in global one-to-group entanglement upon tracing out a single particle. We formulate a computationally efficient variant using tangle and negativity to ensure non-vanishing values for W-class states, and rigorously prove it is a valid monotone under local operations and classical communication. In the tripartite regime, the minimum tangle drop is physically equivalent to the minimum pairwise concurrence. We establish an operational framework where the entanglement drop acts as a structural probe: by assessing sensitivity to qubit loss, it identifies inseparable clusters, extracting connectivity fingerprints that uniquely differentiate graph topologies within the same local Clifford equivalence class. Integrating this mapping with classical shadows enables efficient experimental estimation and dynamic tracking of entanglement network evolution. We derive exact analytical solutions for n-qubit W states under environmental noise, revealing robust scaling behaviors. Finally, we acknowledge limitations, noting that diagnostic sensitivity strictly vanishes for highly robust states such as the 5-qubit error-correcting code.
summary: The paper introduces the 'minimum entanglement drop' as a novel and powerful monotone to quantify genuine multipartite entanglement, moving beyond limitations of traditional measures. It functions as a structural probe that can map out the underlying connectivity graph of entangled qubits by measuring sensitivity to particle loss. While highly effective for distinguishing topologies, its diagnostic power is limited by certain highly robust quantum states.
main_problem: The primary challenge is developing a robust, computationally tractable measure for quantifying genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) that satisfies all necessary theoretical postulates.
main_result: The minimum entanglement drop, defined using negativity or tangle, serves as a powerful structural probe capable of differentiating graph topologies and tracking network evolution. However, it fails to detect entanglement in highly robust states like the 5-qubit error-correcting code.
method: The authors propose defining an entanglement monotone based on the minimum reduction (drop) in global one-to-group entanglement when tracing out a single particle. This is formalized using concepts derived from generalized monogamy inequalities and negativity/tangle measures.
model_or_system: The work analyzes general $n$-qubit quantum states, focusing on characterizing their internal connectivity structure (e.g., comparing Line vs. Star graph topologies) and analyzing the evolution of entanglement under environmental noise.
key_observables: Minimum entanglement drop ($D_{\min}$), minimum negativity drop ($	ext{D}_{S_{q_1}}$), Tangle ($	au$), Negativity ($\mathcal{N}$), and Concurrence ($C$).
important_parameters: Number of qubits ($n$), noise parameter ($\gamma$), and the specific graph topology (Line vs. Star).
main_assumptions: The method is primarily a heuristic structural probe, and its diagnostic sensitivity vanishes for certain highly robust, symmetrically correlated states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how the minimum drop uniquely reveals underlying graph topologies (e.g., distinguishing Line from Star graphs) and show the analytical scaling of $D_{\min}$ for noisy W states versus particle number or noise strength.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the limitations of existing measures, proposing the minimum entanglement drop as a novel monotone, rigorously proving its properties (especially in the tripartite case), demonstrating its utility as a structural probe to map connectivity fingerprints, and finally analyzing its performance on specific state classes like W states under noise.
why_interesting: This work provides advanced diagnostic tools for characterizing complex quantum correlations beyond simple scalar measures. The focus on topological fingerprinting makes it highly relevant for understanding entanglement in physical architectures or noisy quantum channels.
